FOREWORD

was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 10 August 1'381, after the draft finalized by the Electroplating Cheiiiic~als Sectional Committee h:~tl been approved by the Chemical Division Council.

0.2 General applications of rhodium plating in the industrial field are well known. Essential properties of the electro-deposited rhodium metal are high hardness ( hence good wear-resistance) and resistance to corrosion and tarnishing along with good reflectivity. Rhodium elcctrodeposits ha\e been used in the jewellery trade for many years for Rhodium is also used in the in-prin(erl protecting silver from tarnishing. electronic circuitry, where wiping contacts are provided. In rcccnt times, the main use of rhodium has been for electrical, sliding contacts and contacts required to operate after periods of idleness. In the fields of electronics and telecommunications, whcrc cltsc:tricxl signals are small and voltages insufficient to break down tarnish films on silver or base metal contacts, rhodium deposit is used. Rhodium is also used for shorttime protection in high temperature work. `I'hc thickness of rhodium plating in such cases is generally of the order of 2'5 to 5 microiiictcrs ( pm ): Thicker plating of rhodium ( about 50 lrn ) is used on iridium However, deposits thicker than 12.5 i1.m are rarely used, since crucibles. rhodium is one of the lighter metals in the platinum grouli ( ICL) 12.4 ). 0.3 A number of plating baths are used for rhodium plating. The commercial baths are fairly strong acid solutious of rhodium phosphate or rhodium snlphate. Sulphamic and fluoboric acids are also used for preparing rhodium plating baths, btit they are more of ac:iclemic interest. lcor deposits for protection of jewellery, rhodium phosphate solution is used, while for industrial use, rhodium sulphate solution is preferred. Sometimes phospllate-sulphate batlls are a.lso used fog- depositing rhodium. Rhodium can be directly plated on brass, nickel, nickel-silver, phosphorBecause of the acid content of the bath bronze, beryllium, copper, etc. and the position of rhodium in the electrochemical series, it cannot be plated directly on to iron, steel, zinc, aluminiuru, lead or tin :trid, on these therefore, a preliminary deposit of xil\cr is usually ncxlcd The electro-tleposited rhodium has a hardness of about BOO VPN. metals.

A-5.2 Procedure -To the filtrate preserved in A-3.2, add 5 ml each of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acid. Boil the solution and reduce the volume to about 40 ml. Cool and dilute with water to about 100 ml. Add 5 to 10 drops of phenolphthalein indicator solution followed by ammonium hydroxide slowly with stirring until the colour of the solution changes to pink. Slowly add concentrated hydrochloric acid drop by drop until the pink colour disappears and then add 10 ml of the acid in excess. Add 5 g of ammonium acetate and stir in 50 ml of the magnesia mixture. Heat to boiling and slowly add ammonium hydroxide until the solution turns pink again. Stir the solution for about 5 min until the precipitate which first forms becomes finely crystalline in structure. Cool to room temperature and add ammonium hydroxide equivalent to one-fifth of the volume of the solution. Allow to stand for at least 4 h or overnight. Filter through a hard filter paper ( Whatman No. 44 is suitable ), washing the precipitate with 10 ml portions of cold dilute ammonia till free f~l-omchloride. Moisten the filter paper with ammonium nitrate solution, dry the precipitate in it tared platinum crucible. Char the paper slowly, burn off carbon at as low n tcmpcrature as possible with free ;IcceSS of air. Finally ignite to 1 000 to 1 100�C: over a rneker burner Cool in a desiccator and weigh to a constant mass. for 20 to 30 min.
